concept.body: Midsegment = the segment joining the MIDPOINTS of two sides. Two guarantees: (1) PARALLEL to the third side; (2) HALF its length. So third side = 2 × midsegment, and midsegment = ½ × third side. Double one way, halve the other.

explanationVariants: The midsegment is half the third side: 20 ÷ 2 = 10.

widget.prompt: The third side of a triangle is 20. How long is the midsegment parallel to it?

commonErrors.feedback: 40 doubles it — the midsegment is HALF the third side: 20 ÷ 2 = 10.
20 is the third side itself. The midsegment is half: 20 ÷ 2 = 10.

steps.body: Join the **midpoints** of two sides of a triangle and you get a **midsegment** with two striking properties: it's **parallel** to the third side, and it's exactly **half** its length. One little segment, two guarantees — proved with congruent triangles or coordinates.

widget.prompt: The join is locked to the midpoints of the two legs. Drag the apex and watch the midsegment's length against the 18-unit base.
widget.constraintFeedback: You released the lock — the join is no longer between the two midpoints, so its length has nothing to do with the base any more. Lock it again before reading the midsegment.
widget.successFeedback: 9 — exactly half of 18, at every apex angle you tried. The midsegment is not close to half the base; it IS half the base, always, because it is built from the two midpoints and nothing else.
widget.criterionFeedback: The apex angle is what moves here — the criterion itself is not in question.
widget.angleFeedback: The base and the midsegment relationship hold at every angle — bring the apex to 70° to match the target reading.
widget.evidenceFeedback: Try the apex at a few different angles first — one drag is not evidence that the ratio always holds.

predict.prompt: The midsegment joins the MIDPOINTS of two sides. Compared to the 18-unit base it parallels, it will be…

options.label: The same length — parallel means equal
It depends on the triangle's shape

predict.reveal: Cutting both sides at their midpoints creates a small triangle similar to the whole with ratio 1/2 (SAS about the apex), so the midsegment is always exactly half its parallel side — 9 here, and in every triangle, whatever its shape.

explanationVariants: A midsegment is parallel to the third side AND half its length — both hold at once.
The midpoint-to-midpoint segment runs parallel to the base and measures half of it.

widget.prompt: A midsegment of a triangle is guaranteed to be…

options.label: parallel to the third side and half its length
options.feedback: Both properties come together: the midsegment parallels the third side and is exactly half as long.

options.label: perpendicular to the third side
options.feedback: It's PARALLEL to the third side, not perpendicular — they never meet at a right angle in general.

options.label: equal in length to the third side
options.feedback: It's HALF the third side, not equal — joining midpoints shrinks it by exactly a factor of two.

options.label: half the length but not parallel
options.feedback: It's half AND parallel — both hold. The parallelism is as guaranteed as the halving.

steps.body: Why half and parallel? Coordinates make it clean: place the base on the x-axis and compute the two midpoints. Their difference is exactly half the base vector, and its y-component is zero — so the midsegment is parallel and half-length. A congruence proof reaches the same conclusion.

widget.prompt: A midsegment measures 7. How long is the third side of the triangle (the side it's parallel to)?

commonErrors.feedback: 7 is the MIDSEGMENT. The third side is DOUBLE: 7 × 2 = 14.
3.5 halves it the wrong way — the midsegment is half the BASE, so the base is 7 × 2 = 14.

widget.fallbackFeedback: The third side is twice the midsegment: 7 × 2 = 14.

explanationVariants: Connecting all three midpoints makes a middle triangle with each side half the original — so its perimeter is half too.
Three midsegments, each half a side, form a triangle with half the perimeter.

widget.prompt: A triangle has perimeter 24. Connecting all three side-midpoints forms a smaller triangle. What is its perimeter?

commonErrors.feedback: 24 is the ORIGINAL perimeter. Each midsegment is half a side, so the inner perimeter is half: 24 ÷ 2 = 12.
48 doubles it — the midpoint triangle is SMALLER. Each side halves, so the perimeter is 24 ÷ 2 = 12.

widget.fallbackFeedback: Each side halves, so the perimeter halves: 24 ÷ 2 = 12.

steps.body: The three midsegments split a triangle into **four** smaller triangles, all congruent to each other and each **similar** to the original at half scale. The middle one is flipped; the three corner ones are translates. It's a tidy self-similar tiling that the midsegment properties guarantee.

widget.prompt: Drawing all three midsegments divides a triangle into how many smaller triangles?

commonErrors.feedback: 2 comes from drawing just ONE midsegment. All THREE midsegments make 4 triangles.
3 counts only the corner triangles and forgets the flipped middle one: 3 + 1 = 4.

widget.fallbackFeedback: Three midsegments create 4 congruent smaller triangles.

hints: The midsegment is half the third side — set up that relationship.
If the midsegment is (2x + 1) and the third side is 22, then 2x + 1 = 22 ÷ 2.
explanationVariants: The midsegment equals half the base: 2x + 1 = 22 ÷ 2 = 11 → 2x = 10 → x = 5.
Set the midsegment to half the third side: 2x + 1 = 11, so x = 5.

widget.prompt: A midsegment measures (2x + 1) and the side it's parallel to measures 22. Find x.

commonErrors.feedback: 11 is the midsegment's LENGTH (half of 22), not x. Since 2x + 1 = 11, solve: x = 5.
10.5 = 22/2 − ... miscomputes. The midsegment is 22 ÷ 2 = 11, so 2x + 1 = 11 gives x = 5.

takeaways: A midsegment joins two side-midpoints; it's parallel to the third side and half its length.
The third side is double the midsegment; the midpoint triangle has half the perimeter.
Three midsegments split a triangle into four congruent half-scale triangles.
